title: Remarks at Chehalis, Washington
paragraphs: Mr. Chairman; and you, My Fellow Americans: Men and Women of Southwestern Washington:

It is a great pleasure to greet you and to be greeted by the men of the Grand Army, the men to whom we owe it that there is a country, that there is the chance of a President feeling just exactly as much at home on the Pacific as on the Atlantic. (Applause) No wonder the people of Washington have shown themselves true to the practices and principles of the men who fought in the great war. I have just been introduced to two of your fellow citizens, the father and mother of one of the gallant young fellows who in the Philippines captured Aguinaldo (Cheers and applause); and with men such as you and with two of your citizens the father and mother of a boy like that, of course you are expansionists. If you were not I would want to know what was the matter with you. (Applause)

In greeting all of you, and particularly the veterans, I wish to say a special word of pleasure at meeting the children. I am sure they are all right and I know their lungs are all right. (Applause) I congratulate Washington on its agriculture, its commerce, its lumber, its mines, upon all that it produces, but most of all upon its crop of children. (Applause) I have just one word to say to the children. I believe in play and I believe in work. While you play, play hard, and when you work do not play at all. (Applause) That is pretty fair advice for the elder folks too. I like to see people have a good time. I believe in their having a good time; and the very surest way in life not to have it is to try to make a life business of having it. (Applause)The most wretched creatures I have ever met were those who had made up their minds that they were going to have nothing but pleasure out of life. The only life worth living in the long run is the life of effort, the life of striving to accomplish something; and the man or woman who makes up his or her mind that the thing to do is to endeavor only to have a soft and easy time and to shirk duty is not only sure to be a poor citizen but a pretty unhappy one in addition.

You men of the great civil war as you look back in your lives what you most feel pride in is not the days of ease, not the days when things went [?] smoothly, but when in your youth you deliberately chose a life of toil, [?] of effort, of risk, of danger, and were willing to venture all that life had [?] and life itself, because you felt in you the lift of spirit that drove you onward to conquer or to die. That is what you look back upon. (Applause) When you went to the civil war you endured and knew you had to endure every kind of fatigue and hardship. You remember the days when you marched under the heat of the southern sun, the days when at noon a blanket was so heavy that if you were a recruit you threw it away, and at midnight you wished you had two-- you faced it all because you had in you the stuff which recognized in an obstacle not something to be shirked, but something to be conquered. It is just so in civil life. The life worth living is the life which strives and wins, not the life that shrinks from difficulty. The nation of the future will succeed just in proportion as the children of to-day are brought up to feel that life is not something in which ease, safety, comfort, are to be the first considerations; but that in life the first consideration is to endeavor to find something worth doing and to do it well. That is what makes work worth doing-- to do it well in war, to do it well in peace. The lofty nation, the nation that leaves its mark deep in the history of our race, is the nation which dares to be great. I pity no man because he has to work. I pity with the pity that is akin to contempt the man who in our country does not work. Such a man has no true place in our civilization, and I do not care from which end of the social scale he comes. (Applause) If he comes from one end he is technically termed a hobo. If he comes from the other I do not know what his technical term is, but he is just as useless and not one shade happier. No real enjoyment can come to any man worth calling a man unless it comes as the sequel of a life well lived [?], of work well done. The men from '61 to '65 who suffered most, who had the hardest work to do, the greatest risk to encounter, the greatest fatigue to endure, were the men to be envied more than any others in our history-- the men who fought to a finish the great civil war. So it is in civil life. The men we admire and respect, the men whose careers we seek to emulate, are the men who do hard work worth doing and do it well. What type of work it is does not matter, if only it is work that ought to be done and is well done.

That is the fundamental law of our citizenship, the law of brotherhood, the recognition by each man of his fellow's work if that work is honorable and honorably [?] done. It is just as it is in the Grand Army. The man is a comrade whether he was a lieutenant-general or whether he was an eighteen year old recruit provided that each of them did his work well. If the man worthily performed his part you admit him to full privileges of comradeship in every way. And now I meet in the highest positions in the land men who in those four years carried muskets or sabers in the army of the union. In civil life I ask that the same principle be applied, that the same standard of judgment be the one used, that we recognize the indispensability of the thousand occupations in our country and that each man, employer or employed, farmer or townsman, mechanic, wageworker, lawyer, business man, whatever his work be, whoever he be, that he be treated absolutely on his worth as a man, and be judged accordingly as he does his work well. If we apply that principle honestly and in good faith we shall succeed, and only by so applying it can we succeed.

I am glad to have seen you. I greet you, men and women of this great state, a state mighty already, and infinitely mightier in the future. I wish you well. I am proud of you as citizens of the great American republic. (Cheers and applause)
